title: Judgment Against the Nations
summary: These passages do not describe one campaign. Isaiah 13 addresses Babylon and depicts the Medes as agents of its downfall; Jeremiah 46:1–12 turns to Egypt’s defeat at Carchemish. Amos names neighboring peoples and ties its warnings to acts of cruelty, while Obadiah focuses on Edom’s violence toward Judah. Nahum denounces Nineveh, and Zephaniah names a wider set of neighbors and powers. Read together, the oracles show that the prophets hold nations beyond Israel and Judah accountable, while each passage names its own target and grounds.
historical_context: The references point to different places and situations. Isaiah 13 names Babylon and the Medes; Jeremiah 46 identifies the Egyptian army at Carchemish. Amos 1:3–15 lists Aram, Philistia, Tyre, Edom, and Ammon, while Obadiah centers on Edom and Nahum on Nineveh. Zephaniah 2 names several neighboring peoples and Assyria. The passages are prophetic portrayals of judgment, not a single historical report, and they do not supply a shared date for all these oracles.
literary_context: The collection uses several forms of prophetic address. Amos repeats the formula ‘for three transgressions … and for four’ as it moves from one nation to another, and it names the violence behind each warning. Obadiah addresses Edom directly; Nahum uses a taunt against Nineveh; and Zephaniah 2 moves through a list of peoples and cities. These repeated and varied forms give the oracles a shared concern with accountability without making their accusations interchangeable.
covenantal_significance: These passages place neighboring and imperial powers within the same moral horizon as Israel and Judah. The named charges include cruelty, taking captives, betrayal, violence, and pride; political strength does not make a nation immune from judgment. The passages also speak to distinct peoples in distinct settings, so their shared theme should not be used to flatten the specific accusation or historical horizon of any one oracle.
canonical_role: Judgment Against the Nations serves as a prophetic anchor, connecting oracle context, canonical development, and related fulfillment or restoration themes.

interpretive_notes.note: Read the oracle first in its own historical setting.
Prophetic speech is covenantal proclamation before it is prediction.
